The male claims a patch and starts the nest, then dips, tumbles and calls to win a mate.
Fashionable ladies once wore its long plumes on their hats, and the hunt left its numbers dangerously low.

tagline.text: The small white heron that shuffles its supper into view.

facts.text: The willow flycatcher is a small insect-eating, migrant bird of the tyrant flycatcher family native to North America.
Willow flycatchers are generalist insectivores, and the insects which comprise their diet vary substantially across different habitats.
Their song is the only reliable method to tell them apart in the field.
They make a cup nest in a vertical fork in a shrub or tree.
The call is a dry whit.
The section of the book containing the willow flycatcher was published in 1828.
Adults have brown-olive upperparts, darker on the wings and tail, with whitish underparts; they have an indistinct white eye ring, white wing bars and a small bill.
The breast is washed with olive-gray.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 20 cm from its wing length.

It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Whit!
A dry little call drifts out of the shrubland.
There a small brown-olive bird sits perched, white bars on its wings.
It eats insects of many kinds, and its meal changes from one place to the next.
In a fork that stands straight up in a shrub or tree, it shapes a cup for a nest.
Yet its plain coat will not give it away; only its song tells it apart for certain.

tagline.text: Listen close: only its song tells it true.

facts.text: The rusty blackbird is a medium-sized New World blackbird, closely related to grackles.
Rusty blackbirds forage on wet ground or in shallow water, mainly eating insects, crustaceans, small fish during the breeding season.
Birds usually nest at the edge of ponds and wetlands with the cup nest located in a tree or dense shrub, often over the water.
In winter, their diet is more flexible, and contains grains and other seeds.
It is a bird that prefers wet forested areas, breeding in the boreal forest and muskeg across northern Canada, and migrating southeast to the United States during winter.
Their breeding habitat is wet temperate coniferous forests and muskeg across Canada, New England, the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, the Adirondack Mountains in New York and Alaska.
The habitat loss is likely due to multiple factors, including development for oil, gas, and mining industries, hydroelectric projects, and the clearing of forests for forestry.
Rusty blackbirds have declined significantly in recent decades.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 34 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 60 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.

The IUCN Red List rates it Vulnerable.

sentences.text: Deep in the muskeg and wet boreal forest of the far north, it raises its young.
It wades the shallows and soggy edges, taking insects, crustaceans and small fish.
Its cup nest sits in a tree or shrub at the pond's edge, often over the water.
When winter comes, it travels southeast to the United States and turns to grains and seeds.
But its wet woods fall to oil, gas, mining and logging, and its numbers have dropped sharply.

tagline.text: A wader of northern pools, growing rare as its woods vanish.

facts.text: The merlin is a small species of falcon from the Northern Hemisphere, with numerous subspecies throughout North America and Eurasia.
A bird of prey, the merlin breeds in the northern Holarctic; some migrate to subtropical and northern tropical regions in winter.
In Europe, merlins roost communally in winter, often with hen harriers.
In moorland—particularly in the UK—the female will usually make a shallow scrape in dense heather to use as a nest.

Ground-nesting populations in moorland have a preference for tall heather, and are thus susceptible to overmanagement by burning vast tracts instead of creating a habitat mosaic containing old and new growth.
Nestlings are covered in pale buff down feathers, shading to whitish on the belly.
They are swift fliers and skilled hunters, which specialize in preying on small birds in the size range of sparrows to doves and medium-sized shorebirds.
In North America, communal roosting is rare.
Its wingspan is about 60 cm.
It weighs about 188 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a cavity, an old nest another bird built or a scrape on the ground.
It lays 3 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Deep in tall moorland heather, the mother makes her nest, no more than a shallow scrape.
Her young wear pale buff down, fading to whitish on the belly.
Grown, they become swift fliers and skilled hunters, taking small birds from sparrows to doves, and medium-sized shorebirds too.
In winter some travel to warmer lands, and in Europe they roost together, often with hen harriers.
Burn the heather in vast tracts, and those ground nests are put at risk.

tagline.text: A small, swift hunter who nests in the tall heather.

facts.text: The peregrine falcon, also referred to simply as the peregrine, is a bird of prey in the family Falconidae known for its speed.
In mild-winter regions, it is usually a permanent resident, and some individuals, especially adult males, will remain on the breeding territory.
A pair mates for life and returns to the same nesting spot annually.
It is likely the name was used as juvenile birds were taken while journeying to their breeding location, as falcon nests are often difficult to get at.
Peregrines now breed in many mountainous and coastal areas, especially in the west and north, and nest in some urban areas, capitalising on the urban feral pigeon populations for food.
The upper beak is notched near the tip, an adaptation which enables falcons to kill prey by severing the spinal column at the neck.
Although its diet consists almost exclusively of medium-sized birds, the peregrine will sometimes hunt small mammals, small reptiles, or even insects.
The peregrine falcon's diet varies greatly and is adapted to available prey in different regions.
Its wingspan is about 94 cm.
It weighs about 760 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in grassland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time in the air.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On mountains and coasts, and now in some cities, the peregrine makes its home.
A bird of prey known for its speed, it hunts mostly medium-sized birds, and in town the feral pigeons feed it.
Its upper beak is notched near the tip, made for cutting the spine at the neck.
A pair mates for life and returns each year to the same nesting spot.

tagline.text: Swift hunter of cliff, coast and city, true to one nest.

facts.text: The American kestrel is the smallest and most common falcon in the Americas.
The American kestrel usually hunts in an energy-conserving fashion by perching and scanning the ground for prey to ambush, though it also hunts from the air.
A kestrel's habitat must include perches, open space for hunting, and cavities for nesting.
In migratory populations, the males arrive at the breeding ground before females, then the female selects a mate.
The "whine" call is primarily associated with feeding but is also uttered during copulation.
Several other colloquial names for the kestrel are also in use, including grasshopper hawk, due to its diet, and killy hawk, due to its distinct call.
The Peregrine Fund, a leading non-profit organization advancing research and conservation of birds of prey worldwide, launched the American Kestrel Partnership in 2012.
Their less muscular body type is adapted to energy-conserving ambush hunting, rather than spending large amounts of energy-consuming time on the wing and getting into long tail-chases of bird prey.

It weighs about 115 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in grassland.

It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cavity or an old nest another bird built.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Grasshopper hawk, some call it, and killy hawk: one name for its food, one for its call.
The smallest falcon in the Americas does not waste its strength on long chases.
It perches, scans the ground, and waits to ambush, though it can hunt from the air too.
Its less muscular body is made for that patient wait.
Wherever it lives, it needs perches, open ground for hunting, and hollows for nesting.

tagline.text: The little falcon that waits, watches, and strikes.

facts.text: The American coot, also known as a mud hen or pouldeau, is a bird of the family Rallidae.
The American coot is a highly gregarious species, particularly in the winter, when its flocks can number in the thousands.
Coot mate pairings are monogamous throughout their life, given they have a suitable territory.
The American coot has a variety of repeated calls and sounds.
Coot can be used for cooking; it is somewhat popular in Cajun cuisine, for instance as an ingredient for gumbos cooked at home by duck hunters.

Black American coot chicks have conspicuously orange-tipped ornamental plumes covering the front half of their body that are known as "chick ornaments" that eventually get bleached out after six days.
Coots generally build floating nests and lay 8–12 eggs per clutch.

When swimming on the water surface, American coots exhibit a variety of interesting collective formations, including single-file lines, high density synchronized swimming and rotational dynamics, broad arcing formations, and sequential take-off dynamics.
Its wingspan is about 64 cm.
It weighs about 637 g.
It feeds mostly on water plants.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 6 to 15 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Mud hen, some call it, or pouldeau: a bird of the rail family.
In winter the coots crowd together, their flocks sometimes thousands strong.
On the water they move like a drilled band: single-file lines, tight synchronized swimming, broad arcs, and take-offs one after another.
A pair stays together for life, so long as they hold a good territory.
They build their nest to float, and their black chicks wear orange-tipped plumes, called chick ornaments, that soon bleach away.

tagline.text: The mud hen swims in lines, arcs, and crowds.

facts.text: The common loon or great northern diver is a large member of the loon, or diver, family of birds.
Common loons eat a variety of animal prey including fish, crustaceans, insect larvae, molluscs, and occasionally aquatic plant life.
Its clumsiness on land is due to the legs being positioned at the rear of its body; the pelvic muscles are well developed, ideal for swimming but not well-suited for walking.
The common loon's mating system is serially monogamous; breeding pairs jointly defend a territory consisting of an entire small lake or a protected bay within a large lake.
Each of these calls communicates a distinct message.
The voice and appearance of the common loon has made it prominent in several Native American tales.
The European name "diver" comes from the bird's practice of catching fish by diving.
The lakes must be large enough for flight take-off, and provide a large population of small fish.
Its wingspan is about 142 cm.
It weighs about 5 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a mound.
It lays 1 to 3 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On a whole small lake, or a sheltered bay within a large one, a pair keeps its kingdom and guards it together.
It dives to catch its fish, the habit that gave it its European name.
Its legs sit far back on its body, strong for swimming, so on land it stumbles clumsily.
It has many calls, and each one carries its own message.
Its voice and its look have carried it into several Native American tales.

tagline.text: Keeper of the lake, it dives for fish and calls with meaning.

facts.text: The red-throated loon or red-throated diver is a migratory aquatic bird found in the Northern Hemisphere.
Fish form the bulk of its diet, though amphibians, invertebrates, and plant material are sometimes eaten as well.
Young use this method of covering ground when moving from their breeding pools to larger bodies of water, including rivers and the sea.
The female lays two eggs; they are incubated for 24–29 days, primarily by the female.
In flight, when passing conspecifics or circling its own pond, it gives a series of rapid yet rhythmic goose-like cackles—kaa-kaa-kaa or kak-kak-kak, at roughly five calls per second.
Used as a food source since prehistoric times, the red-throated loon is still hunted by indigenous peoples in some parts of the world today.
In contrast to other loons, its main fishing grounds are not the breeding lake, but larger lakes or the sea.
When it first emerges from its egg, the young red-throated loon is covered with fine soft down feathers.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Over a northern pond rings a quick, steady cackle, kak-kak-kak, as the bird circles its own water.
Yet that pond is not where it fishes.
Unlike its kin, it hunts in larger lakes or the sea, and fish fill most of its meals.
Its chicks hatch wrapped in fine, soft down.
Later the young leave their breeding pools for bigger waters too: rivers and the sea.
The pond is a cradle, the story says; the wide water, a table.

tagline.text: It cackles over its pond, but hunts the wide sea.

facts.text: The common yellowthroat is a New World warbler.
Common yellowthroat nests are commonly subject to brood parasitism by the brown-headed cowbird.
Common yellowthroats nest in low vegetation, laying 3–5 eggs in a cup-shaped nest.
The song is a loud twichety twichety twichety twich.
Common yellowthroats here typically migrate to this island during the spring months displaying distinct patterns of movement and stopover ecology.

Linnaeus specified the locality as North America but this was restricted to the state of Maryland by the American Ornithologists' Union in 1931.

sentences.text: "Twichety twichety twichety twich!" rings the loud song of the common yellowthroat, a New World warbler of the wetlands.
When it speaks softly, its call is just a quiet jip.
Low in the plants it builds a cup-shaped nest and lays its eggs.
Yet a stranger often comes calling: the brown-headed cowbird, which leaves its own eggs there for others to raise.
Though lost habitat has thinned its numbers, the singer is still very common.

tagline.text: Loud twichety song, soft jip call, and a nest down low.

facts.text: The American oystercatcher, occasionally called the American pied oystercatcher, is a member of family Haematopodidae.
Originally called the "sea pie", it was renamed in 1731 when naturalist Mark Catesby claimed that he had observed the bird eating oysters.
They nest on beaches on coastal islands and feed on marine invertebrates.
In the 19th century they became locally extinct in the lower northeastern United States due to market hunting and egg collecting.
Historically, the American oystercatcher was hunted to near extinction in the 19th century for plumage and eggs.

Once called the sea pie, it got a new name in 1731, when the naturalist Mark Catesby said he had watched it eat oysters.
Hunted long ago for its feathers and eggs, it came close to vanishing for good.
In winter, flocks gather along the coast from central New Jersey to the Gulf of Mexico.
Still, building and rising seas can take its home.

tagline.text: It nests on the beaches of islands by the sea.

facts.text: The house finch is a North American bird in the finch family.
House finches forage on the ground or in vegetation normally.
Nests are made in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations.
Analyses of nest records from house finches in California spanning more than a century found that egg‐laying occurred significantly earlier in warmer springs.
The mite Pellonyssus reedi is often found on house finch nestlings, particularly for nests later in the season.
Male coloration varies in intensity with the seasons and is derived from the berries and fruits in its diet.
They primarily eat grains, seeds and berries, being voracious consumers of weed seeds such as nettle and dandelion; included are incidental small insects such as aphids.
Sometimes nests abandoned by other birds are used.

sentences.text: Look for the house finch's nest in an opening in a building, a hanging plant, or a cup-shaped outdoor decoration.
Sometimes it simply moves into a nest another bird left behind.
Its feast is grains, seeds and berries, and it greedily gobbles weed seeds like nettle and dandelion, with a stray aphid now and then.
The male wears his meals: his color comes from the berries and fruits he eats, and it deepens and fades with the seasons.

tagline.text: A finch that wears the berries it eats.

facts.text: The bald eagle is a bird of prey found in North America.
It reaches speeds of 56–70 km/h when gliding and flapping, and about 48 km/h while carrying fish.
Bald eagles have high mate fidelity and generally mate for life.
The Pawnee consider eagles as symbols of fertility because their nests are built high off the ground and because they fiercely protect their young.
In March 2024, bald eagles were found nesting in Toronto for the first time.
Bald eagles, like many birds of prey, were especially affected by DDT due to biomagnification.
The highly developed talon of the hind toe is used to pierce the vital areas of prey while it is held immobile by the front toes.
It is found near large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply and old-growth trees for nesting.

sentences.text: Where open water lies wide and old trees stand tall, the bald eagle of North America makes its home.
Its front toes hold the prey still while the great hind talon pierces its vital places.
Even carrying fish, it flies at about 48 kilometres an hour.
A pair, once joined, most often stays together for life.
The Pawnee see eagles as signs of fertility, for their nests sit high off the ground and they fiercely guard their young.

tagline.text: Lord of open water, true to its mate for life.

facts.text: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica.
The barn swallow is a bird of open country that normally nests in man-made structures and consequently has spread with human expansion.
The barn swallow is similar in its habits to other aerial insectivores, including other swallow species and the unrelated swifts.
The male barn swallow returns to the breeding grounds before the females and selects a nest site, which is then advertised to females with a circling flight and song.
Males sing to defend small territories and to attract mates.
The barn swallow is an attractive bird that feeds on flying insects and has therefore been tolerated by humans when it shares their buildings for nesting.

The same individuals often breed at the same site year after year, although settlement choices have been experimentally shown to be predicted by nest availability rather than any characteristics of available mates.
Hot dry summers will reduce the availability of insect food for chicks.

sentences.text: The male swallow returns to the breeding grounds before the females and picks a nest site.

A bird of open country, he nests in what people build, and so he has spread as people spread.
People let him share their buildings, for he eats flying insects.
Year after year, the same birds often return to the same place, drawn more by an open nest than a mate.

tagline.text: He picks the nest, then circles it in song.

facts.text: The wood thrush is a North American passerine bird in the family Turdidae and is the only species placed in the genus Hylocichla.
The song of the male is often cited as being the most beautiful in North America.
The wood thrush is primarily solitary, but occasionally forms mixed-species flocks in the winter.
The pairs will perch together and feed each other in between flights.
The wood thrush has been reported to have one of the most beautiful songs of North American birds.
The wood thrush can breed in habitat patches as small as 0.4 hectares, but it runs the risk of higher predation and nest parasitism.
Forest fragmentation in North American forests has resulted in both increased nest predation and increased cowbird parasitism, significantly reducing their reproductive success.
The wood thrush is an omnivore, and feeds preferentially on soil invertebrates and larvae, but will also eat fruits.

sentences.text: In North American forests, a lone singer keeps to itself, joining mixed flocks only now and then in winter.
It eats the small creatures of the soil and their larvae, and fruit as well.
Pairs perch together and feed each other between flights.
But its fame is the male's song, often called the most beautiful in North America.
As the forests break into smaller pieces, more of its nests are troubled by predators and cowbirds.

tagline.text: A lone singer whose song is called the loveliest of all.

facts.text: The Baltimore oriole is a small icterid blackbird common in eastern North America as a migratory breeding bird.
Baltimore orioles forage in trees and shrubs, also making short flights to catch insects.
In the spring, males establish a territory and then display to females by singing and chattering while hopping from perch to perch in front of them.
Male orioles sing to proclaim and protect territory.
Among other causes Dutch elm disease destroyed a meaningful amount of their favorite nesting locations: elm trees.

In spring the male claims a territory and sings to guard it.

Yet she sings too, and when she guards her nest she gives a fierce screech.

facts.text: The dark-eyed junco is a species of junco, a group of small, grayish New World sparrows.

sentences.text: In winter, the dark-eyed junco keeps close to towns, and at many feeders it is the most common bird of all.

tagline.text: The small gray sparrow that crowds the winter feeder

facts.text: The ring-billed gull is a medium-sized gull native to North America, breeding in Canada and the northern Contiguous United States, and wintering mainly in the United States and northern Mexico.

facts.text: The lesser black-backed gull is a large gull that breeds on the Atlantic and Arctic coasts of Europe.

tagline.text: It sinks from danger, then watches with only its head showing.

facts.text: The black-capped chickadee is a small, nonmigratory, North American passerine bird that lives in deciduous and mixed forests.
The bird is well known for its vocalizations, including its fee-bee song and its chick-a-dee-dee-dee call, from which it derives its name.
Insects form a large part of their diet in summer.
In the spring, the winter flocks will disperse into the constituent pairs.
One of the most recognizable sounds produced, particularly by the males, is the two-note fee-bee song.
Black-capped chickadees have a slower, hoarser, two-part song, whereas Carolina chickadees have a three-part song.
It feeds primarily on insects and seeds, and is known for its ability to cache food for use during the winter.
The birds hop along tree branches searching for food, sometimes hanging upside down or hovering; they may make short flights to catch insects in the air.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 20 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 11 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays 6 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Upside down on a branch in the leafy woods, a small singer hangs, searching for food.
It hops, it hovers, it darts out on short flights to snatch insects from the air.
It never leaves its home woods, and it hides food away to eat in winter.
In spring the winter flocks break into pairs, and the males most of all sing a slow, hoarse fee-bee.
Yet the name it carries comes from another call: chick-a-dee-dee-dee.

tagline.text: It hangs upside down to hunt and hides food for winter.

facts.text: The blue-gray gnatcatcher is a very small gnatcatcher native to North America.
Blue-gray gnatcatchers prefer humid areas with large leaves, woodlands, and more open sandy areas with sparse trees where they mainly eat insects, insect eggs, and spiders.
The incubation period is 10–15 days for both sexes, where the female lays a clutch of 4–5 eggs.
The songs are often heard on breeding grounds, and occasionally heard other times of the year.
The males often work to build nests, help incubate and raise the young, as well as feed the children.
The blue-gray gnatcatcher can raise up to two broods in a season.
The blue-gray gnatcatcher's breeding habitat includes open deciduous woods and shrublands in southern Ontario, the eastern and southwestern United States, and Mexico.
Adult males are blue-gray on the upperparts with white underparts, slender dark bill, and a long black tail edged in white.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 16 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 5.8 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In open woods and shrublands from southern Ontario to Mexico, a very small blue-gray bird keeps house.
The male does not leave the work to his mate: he often helps build the nest, takes turns on the eggs, and feeds the young.
Together they may raise two broods in one season.
Insects, insect eggs and spiders fill their busy days, and their songs are often heard on these breeding grounds.

tagline.text: A tiny blue-gray father who builds, sits, and feeds.

facts.text: The boat-tailed grackle is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae found as a permanent resident on the coasts of the Southeastern and Mid-Atlantic United States.
They forage on the ground, in shallow water, or in shrubs; they will steal food from other birds, animals, or humans.
The nest is a well-concealed cup in trees and shrubs near water; the average clutch size is just over three eggs.
Its song is a harsh jeeb, and it has a variety of typically grackle-like chatters and squeaks.
Urban boat-tailed grackle populations can be found foraging in trash bins, parking lots, and outdoor restaurant patios.
Young males are black but lack the adult's iridescence.
They are omnivorous opportunistic feeders, eating insects, crustaceans, minnows, frogs, eggs, berries, seeds, grain, and even small birds.
Their call lacks of whistles and clucks typical of the great-tailed grackle.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 46 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 151 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Along the southeastern and Mid-Atlantic coasts, a bold forager keeps its home all year round.
It hunts on the ground, in shallow water and in shrubs, and it will steal a meal from birds, animals or people.
Insects, minnows, frogs, eggs, berries, seeds and grain, even small birds: it refuses almost nothing.
In town it combs trash bins, parking lots and restaurant patios.
Its song is a harsh jeeb, threaded with chatters and squeaks.

tagline.text: The coast's bold thief, eating nearly anything it finds.

facts.text: The common grackle is an icterid bird found in large numbers through much of North America.
The common grackle forages on the ground, in shallow water, or in shrubs; it may steal food from other birds.
In the breeding season, males tip their heads back and fluff up feathers to display and keep other males away.
The grackle's song is particularly harsh, especially when these birds, in a flock, are calling.
Common grackles are considered to be a serious threat to crops by some, and are notoriously difficult to control; this usually requires the use of hawks or similar large birds of prey.
The nest is a well-concealed cup in dense trees or shrubs, usually near water; sometimes, the common grackle nests in cavities or in man-made structures.
It is omnivorous, eating insects, minnows, frogs, eggs, berries, seeds, grain, and even small birds and rodents.
Songs vary from year-round chewink chewink to a more complex breeding season ooo whew, whew, whew, whew, whew call that gets faster and faster and ends with a loud crewhewwhew!

The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: On the ground, in shallow water, in the shrubs, it hunts its meals, and it will snatch food from other birds as well.
It eats insects, minnows, frogs, berries, grain, even small birds.
In the breeding season, a male tips his head back and fluffs his feathers to keep other males away.
That season his song builds: ooo whew, whew, whew, faster and faster, ending in a loud crewhewwhew!
In a calling flock, the sound is harsh indeed.

tagline.text: Rough song, wide appetite, and a habit of stealing food.

facts.text: The clapper rail is a member of the rail family, Rallidae.
They search for food while walking, sometimes probing with their long bills, in shallow water or mud.

sentences.text: Mud underfoot, marsh all around: this large brown walker keeps to the saltmarshes along Atlantic coasts.

Where the plants grow thick, it heaps dry grasses into a large platform on the ground.
There as many as sixteen eggs may lie.
And it roams widely across its range; few return to the place of their birth, the males least of all.

tagline.text: A brown wanderer, probing the saltmarsh mud.

facts.text: The golden-crowned kinglet is a very small songbird in the family Regulidae that lives throughout much of North America.
The golden-crowned kinglet is insectivorous, foraging in trees or shrubs, where it eats insects, insect eggs and spiders.
It produces a series of high-pitched calls on a single note, and tends not to fear human approach.

R. s. olivaceus, breeding from coastal southeastern Alaska to southwestern Oregon, wintering to Idaho and southwestern California.

sentences.text: In coniferous forests from Canada to Central America, a very small songbird hunts through trees and shrubs.
It seeks out insects, insect eggs and spiders.
Its voice is a string of high-pitched calls, all sung on one single note.
It wears a yellow crown edged in black, with a black stripe through each eye.
And when people come near, this tiny crowned hunter tends not to fear them.

tagline.text: A tiny crowned hunter of the conifer woods.

facts.text: The black skimmer is a tern-like seabird, one of three similar bird species in the skimmer genus Rynchops in the gull family Laridae.

Fish prey species include Odontesthes argentinenesis, Brevoortia aurea, Anchoa marinii, Lycengraulis grossidens, Engraulis anchoita, Pomatomus saltatrix, Mugil cephalus, Fundulus heteroclitus, Anchoa mitchilli and Odontesthes incisa.

sentences.text: Kak-kak-kak, barks a tern-like seabird across North and South America.
It nests in a shallow scrape on the ground.
The chicks are up and about the moment they hatch, yet they lie unnoticed in the scrape while the parents shade them from the heat.
Mothers do most of the feeding, though fathers have been seen bringing larger prey to older chicks.
Meals come almost only by day, for sometimes every grown bird leaves the colony to fish.

tagline.text: A barking cry, a shaded scrape, and meals mostly by daylight.

facts.text: The eastern phoebe is a small passerine bird.
Phoebe is an alternative name for the Roman moon goddess Diana, but it may also have been chosen to imitate the bird's call.
Insects make up a great majority of its summer diet; included are many small wasps, bees, beetles, flies, true bugs, and grasshoppers.
The eastern phoebe's call is a sharp chip, and the song, from which it may get its name, is fee-bee.
Small fruits and berries are eaten often during the cooler months.
The eastern phoebe often nests on human structures such as bridges and buildings.
The breeding habitat is open woodland, farmland, and suburbs, often near water.

sentences.text: Fee-bee, fee-bee: so the small singer sings, and from that song, one telling goes, it takes its name.
Another telling hears in the name the Roman moon goddess Diana, who was also called Phoebe.
It keeps near water, in open woods, farmland and suburbs, and often builds its nest on bridges and buildings.
Through summer it lives on insects: small wasps and bees, beetles, flies and grasshoppers.
In the cooler months it often eats small fruits and berries.

tagline.text: Fee-bee from the bridge: a song that may be a name.

facts.text: Woodcocks spend most of their time on the ground in brushy, young-forest habitats, where the birds' brown, black, and gray plumage provides excellent camouflage.
They do most of their feeding in places where the soil is moist.
The male's ground call is a short, buzzy peent.
In late summer, some woodcocks roost on the ground at night in large openings among sparse, patchy vegetation.
Creating young-forest habitat for American woodcocks helps more than 50 other species of wildlife that need early successional habitat during part or all of their lifecycles.
They forage by probing in soft soil in thickets, where they usually remain well-hidden.
After sounding a series of ground calls, the male takes off and flies from 50 to 100 yd into the air.

sentences.text: In brushy young forest, a brown, black and gray bird keeps to the ground, and its feathers hide it well.
It feeds where the soil is moist, probing soft earth in thickets, where it usually stays well hidden.
In springtime, from old fields, pastures and roadsides, the male sounds his short, buzzy peent.
After a series of these calls, he takes off and climbs up to 100 yards into the air.

tagline.text: Hidden in the thicket, it buzzes peent and climbs the sky.

facts.text: The ovenbird is a small songbird of the New World warbler family Parulidae.
Ovenbirds forage on the ground in dead leaves, sometimes hovering or catching insects in flight.
The nest, referred to as the "oven", is a domed structure placed on the ground, woven from vegetation, and containing a side entrance.
The main song of the ovenbird is a series of strident, relatively low-pitched, bisyallabic motives repeated without pause about eight times and increasing in volume.
For foraging, it prefers woodland with abundant undergrowth of shrubs; essentially, it thrives best in a mix of primary and secondary forest.
The female usually lays 4–5 eggs speckled with brown or gray.
The call Archived 2010-06-08 at the Wayback Machine is a variably pitched, sharp "chik!" Some variations recall the common call note of a downy woodpecker.
The birds are territorial all year round, occurring either singly or as mated pairs, for a short time accompanied by their young.
Its wingspan is about 24 cm.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Down on the woodland floor, among dead leaves, a small songbird goes about its work.
It hunts there, sometimes hovering, sometimes catching insects in flight.
On that same ground it weaves a house of plants, a dome with a door in its side, and this house is called the oven.
Inside, the female lays eggs speckled with brown or gray.
Then comes the song: a harsh, low pair of notes, said again and again without pause, louder each time.

tagline.text: A woven dome on the ground, with a door in its side.

facts.text: The American yellow warbler, also known as the northern yellow warbler, is a New World warbler.

In the trees, the female leads the building of a small but very sturdy cup nest.
Both parents share the raising of the young, and the young devour many pest insects.
Roughly 60% of their food is caterpillars.

facts.text: The northern parula is a small New World warbler.
The northern parula forages mostly or entirely on arboreal invertebrates.

sentences.text: High in the trees, a tiny hunter picks through the branches for spiders, beetles, caterpillars and ants.
In a mixed flock it is often one of the smallest, beside kinglets and gnatcatchers.

facts.text: The black-throated blue warbler is a small passerine bird of the New World warbler family.
Predominantly insectivorous, the black-throated blue warbler supplements its diet with berries and seeds in winter.
The black-throated blue warbler forages actively in low vegetation, sometimes hovering or catching insects in flight.
He then follows the female while she is foraging or searching for nesting sites.

In winter, berries and seeds join its insect meals.

It tucks its cup in thick shrubs, so near the ground that watchers favor it for learning how its kind live.

facts.text: The yellow-rumped warbler is a North American bird species that can be commonly observed all across the continent.
The yellow-rumped warbler is primarily insectivorous, though the species eats fruit such as juniper berries, especially in winter.
While they are primarily insectivorous, the species is perhaps the most versatile foragers of all warblers.
Audubon's and the myrtle nest in coniferous and mixed woodlands, and lay 4–5 eggs.

facts.text: The palm warbler is a small songbird in the New World warbler family.

facts.text: The chestnut-sided warbler is a New World warbler.

facts.text: The Carolina wren is a species of wren common in the eastern United States, the extreme south of Ontario, Canada, the northeast and southeast of Mexico, and into northern Central America.

facts.text: The brown thrasher, sometimes erroneously called the brown thrush or fox-coloured thrush, is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the New World catbirds and mockingbirds.

facts.text: The willet is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
